name: Takuya Nemoto
title: Venues omitted — where this work was posted, and where it was not | Takuya Nemoto
description: SSRN, PhilArchive, Zenodo and arXiv set side by side by the differences in their published acceptance rules. No venue is ranked below another. Why arXiv was not used, and how that decision changed.
tagline: Where this work was posted, and where it was not. What is compared is the acceptance rules, not the quality of the work they carry. No venue is being ranked below another.

blocks.title: What this page is
blocks.html:
No venue is being ranked below another. What is compared here is the acceptance rules each site publishes, not the quality of the work they carry. The rules differ because what each is trying to take in differs.

This is not a page that orders venues. The only thing that can be ordered is whether a venue suits this particular work. Not posting to a venue that does not suit it is what this page calls omission.

Rules move. arXiv's acceptance rules changed twice in succession, in October 2025 and January 2026. What is written here is as of the date at the top of the page. Changes after that are not reflected.

Every source below was taken from search results. The sites were not opened and read from the working environment (only GitHub is reachable). Nothing is written as "confirmed" that was not confirmed. If a rule is found to be described wrongly here, that line gets corrected.

blocks.title: Where it is posted now
blocks.html:
VenueWhat is thereStanding
ZenodoThe paper PDFs and their bibliographic recordsOf record. A DOI is assigned and the version is fixed
SSRNTwo of the philosophy papersSame text. A way in, not the record
PhilArchiveThree philosophy papersLikewise. This is where readers in the field are

PhilPeopleAuthor informationNot a venue. A directory of philosophers
researchmapA list of outputNot a venue. A researcher database

Which one is authoritative is fixed in canonical-sources.md. Where they disagree, Zenodo is authoritative.

blocks.title: How the gates differ
blocks.html:
VenueWhat the gate looks at
ZenodoNo substantive review. Spam and unlawful material are excluded
Knowledge CommonsMembership registration
HALFormat and affiliation. The content is not read
PhilArchiveThere are stated criteria. Set out in the next section
SSRNEditorial staff screen before posting
arXivEndorsement and moderation. Set out in a later section

Of the venues in use, two have a gate: PhilArchive and SSRN. They hang it differently. SSRN has editorial staff look before it goes up. PhilArchive states its criteria, then has category editors tidy after the fact, reserving the right to reject.

None of these is peer review. Peer review is a procedure in which researchers in the field judge whether the content holds and decide on acceptance. None of the above does that. Nor does having a DOI mean anything was peer reviewed.

blocks.title: The PhilArchive and PhilPeople criteria
blocks.html:
Run by the PhilPapers Foundation. The published criteria are as follows (unconfirmed).

WhatHow it stands
FieldPrimarily philosophy. Non-philosophy only where it is interdisciplinary and of evident interest to philosophers
StandardAll books and articles submitted must meet professional standards
RejectionThe right to reject any submission is reserved
EditorsMore than six hundred researchers are appointed as category editors. Their role is to keep irrelevant or misfiled items out of the categories they hold
ProhibitedThreats and harassment, personal information posted without consent, impersonation

It is not a place where anyone can post anything. The standard is stated, the right of rejection is reserved, and more than six hundred editors tidy after the fact. That is where it differs from Zenodo.

PhilPeople is not a venue but a directory of philosophers as a profession. Registration is free, and unregistered people are included from public institutional information. Claiming an unregistered entry as one's own requires registering. Whether there is a procedure that verifies affiliation cannot be determined from this environment.

The operators themselves say it is not peer review

The stated criterion and the operators' own explanation differ in strength. The submission page says work must be of professional quality. At the launch in October 2017, Bourget and Chalmers wrote the following (unconfirmed).

Papers submitted to PhilArchive are not peer reviewed, although to prevent abuse they are subject to vetting for minimal standards of quality and relevance.

There is a gate. It is not a gate in the sense that specialists passed on whether the argument holds. Both are the operators' own words. Quoting one alone makes it as strong or as weak as one likes. Both are quoted here.

Three separate things

WhatWhat it meansWhere the three papers stand
The work's professional qualityThe submission criterion, stated by the operatorsPassed
The author's professional author statusHolding a doctorate in philosophy, or authoring an article in a journal on PhilPapers' list of most popular journals. Said to be determined algorithmicallyNeither applies
Publication in a peer-reviewed journalResearchers in the field judge whether the content holds and decide on acceptanceNone

Passing the first is not stretched into the second or the third. The site itself keeps the three apart. The default listing is said to be filtered by professional author (unconfirmed). Passing a criterion is not the field accepting the work as professional work.

Where the three papers came from

The three papers were written by self-study. They were not coursework. They were not written under supervision. There was no collaborator. Philosophy is taken at university, but the three papers sit outside that.

Language models were used. Which tools cannot be identified. No record was kept, and the author's memory does not settle it. The errata for the three papers (E5) says so. No single name is given here. Giving one would contradict an errata entry that says the tool cannot be identified.

On that footing, the three are posted on PhilArchive. Two of them passed SSRN's editorial screening.

The bar that was cleared — SSRN

To write that something passed, what it passed has to be fixed in the published wording. Paraphrase makes it weaker or stronger at will, so the wording is given verbatim (all unconfirmed; the originals were not opened).

RequirementThe wordingWhat meeting it amounts to
Subject fitA paper must be part of the world-wide scholarly discourse covered by one or more of SSRN's subject area networksThe subject was taken to belong to the scholarly discourse of one of SSRN's networks
ScholarlinessNon-scholarly items are not normally accepted — articles with no references and some commercial or marketing material are namedSomething with no references does not get through. Two papers did
The stated standardSSRN accepts studies with rigorous methodology and original findings, meeting our posting standardsThis is the standard the policy states. It has to be read together with the row below
FormTitle (English), date written, abstract (English), names, affiliations and email addresses of all authors, rights holder's permission where applicable, PDFAnything missing can be grounds for rejection
Research integrityResearch submissions can be rejected for integrity or editorial reasons at various stages / SSRN does not provide detailed feedback on why a paper may have failed an integrity checkRejection on integrity grounds is possible. No detailed reason is given
Kind of reviewSSRN does not peer review preprints / Staff may edit or query an abstract, and will occasionally reject a submission judged insufficiently scholarlyNeither the soundness of the method nor the substance of the content. What is looked at is whether it holds up as scholarship at all

There is a step inside the published wording. rigorous methodology and original findings and does not peer review are the same operator's words. The first is an acceptance policy, the second a description of the procedure. What the two papers passed is the procedure, not a check that the first was met.

The bar that was cleared — PhilArchive

RequirementThe wordingWhat meeting it amounts to
Subject fitworks of all types (articles, books, dissertations) in all areas of academic philosophy; non-philosophy only where cross-disciplinary and of clear interest to philosophersTreated as lying within academic philosophy
StandardAll books and papers submitted should be of professional qualityA professional standard is required
Right of rejectionreserve the right to reject any submissionsAny submission may be rejected
ProhibitedThreats and harassment, personal information without consent, impersonationNone applies
Tidying afterwardsMore than six hundred category editors keep irrelevant or misfiled items out of their categoriesThis acts after the fact, not before
Kind of reviewnot peer reviewed, although to prevent abuse they are subject to vetting for minimal standards of quality and relevance (the operators, 2017)Not whether the argument holds. What is checked is a minimum of quality and relevance

There is a step here too. professional quality comes from the submission page, minimal standards from the launch announcement. Quoting one alone makes it as strong or as weak as one likes.

The two gates are alike in this: passing one is not a judgement on whether the content holds. What can be claimed as attainment reaches exactly as far as the "what meeting it amounts to" column. Beyond that, the published wording guarantees nothing.

What happened to each of the three

PaperSSRNPhilArchiveDid a gate come down
The Nobility and Exemplarity of the Celibate Individual10.2139/ssrn.7358779NEMTNABoth gates came down — SSRN's screening and PhilArchive's. Submitted before the profile was public
Manifesto of Imperial Selfhood10.2139/ssrn.7358818NEMMOIThe same
Fragmentarian Spiritual IndividualismNot submittedNEMFSIIt did not. It went up the moment the profile became public

One of the three went through no screening at all. "Fragmentarian Spiritual Individualism" went up the moment the account became public. There was no wait, no return, no query. It was never submitted to SSRN. This is the author's testimony. It cannot be checked against a document.

For the other two, a gate did come down on the PhilArchive side. This is the author's testimony. The three are not uniform — same venue, same author, and still two where the gate came down and one where it did not. They are written neither as all passed nor as none passed.

There is an order to it. The two where the gate came down were submitted, and screened, before the PhilPeople profile was made public. The one where it did not went up the moment the profile became public. Same venue, different treatment before and after. This is the author's testimony.

It is not written here that the publication caused it. It may be that the two earlier submissions established who the author was; it may be a difference of timing. What was observed is an order, not a mechanism. Nor was any published procedure seen that names publication as the trigger.

It does not contradict the stated criterion. Reserving a right of rejection and reading everything in advance are different things. But "passed the gate" can only be written where the gate actually came down. For this one paper it did not. Hence "posted".

Where a gate did come down, it is a gate on acceptance. Of the three tiers above, only the first. Neither the second nor the third has been reached. Getting work out by self-study and the field accepting it are different things. Joining them here would be doing the very thing this page warns others against.

What it takes to be able to post

Reading needs no registration. Posting does. As far as has been published, it stands as follows (all unconfirmed).

WhatHow it stands
ReadingReadable without an account
PostingAn account is required. Authors post their own work themselves
Unclaimed entriesUnregistered philosophers are included from public information. Claiming an entry as one's own requires registering
Once the profile is publicVisibility of the doctorate, email address, events and demographics can each be set; the whole profile can be made private. Publications are pulled from PhilPapers, talks from PhilEvents, career events from PhilJobs
The forumsIntended for professional philosophers and graduate students. A 2012 discussion states that posts from those without professional status wait to be ratified by an academic. That is fourteen years old, and whether it still holds has not been checked

No statement that posting becomes possible once the profile goes public appears in the published procedure. That an account is required to post does appear. Publication is nowhere named as the trigger.

On the author's side there is testimony that the treatment differed before and after (the section above). Testimony is not a description of procedure. The two are not put in the same column.

blocks.title: How arXiv differs
blocks.html:
arXiv's acceptance is of a different order from any of the above. As far as has been published, it stands as follows (all unconfirmed).

WhatHow it stands
EndorsementA first-time submitter needs an endorsement from someone who has already submitted in that field
Relaxation by emailSince 21 January 2026, an institutional email address no longer triggers automatic endorsement
Automatic endorsement in mathematicsSince 10 December 2025, an institutional email alone does not suffice in the mathematics categories. Both an institutional email and authorship of a paper accepted into arXiv Mathematics are required
Who may endorseSomeone with two to five papers on arXiv in that domain, submitted between three months and five years ago
Holds and rejectionsAbout 6% of submissions are held, about 2% rejected. Reasons for rejection are as a rule not given
ReclassificationModerators may move a submission to a different category
Reviews and position papersSince October 2025, computer science does not accept them without prior peer review
AI-generated materialHallucinated references or leftover prompt text carry a one-year submission ban

This is not strictness on display. These are rules for narrowing what is taken in. It is run as a place for new results, and the gate is narrow for that reason.

blocks.title: Why it was omitted
blocks.html:
It was not posted to arXiv. The reason does not lie with arXiv. There are three.

First. An endorsement is required. Since January 2026 an institutional email address does not produce one automatically. In the mathematics categories that has held since earlier still, 10 December 2025. Both an institutional email and authorship of a paper accepted into arXiv Mathematics are required. An endorser has to be found individually.

Second. What survives contains no new result. This was not said from outside; the record says it of itself —— what survives is one fact about one operator, at the level of a second- or third-year undergraduate exercise. Posting something that is not a new result to a place for new results does not fit the rules. That is why it was not posted.

Third. There is no occasion to explain how it came about. That the first draft was the output of a language model is written in the record. Disclosing it and posting is not the same as posting with it concealed. But acceptance does not hear individual circumstances. It would mean bringing a history that needs explaining to a place with no occasion to explain it.

On 9 September 2026 the author decided to post it. The three reasons above are not deleted. The first and the third are procedural, and there are ways to deal with them. The second has no way to deal with it. Deciding to post and having a new result are separate things.

The expectation of rejection is written down before the outcome is known. It is in ARXIV.md —— the three forms it could take, the candidate categories, what to state when asking for endorsement, and where the outcome gets written. Even if it is accepted, acceptance is not proof of novelty. arXiv is a gate on acceptance, not peer review.

There is an arXiv author identifier page. arxiv.org/a/0009-0000-1406-0547. This is the page that appears once an ORCID is linked to an arXiv user record, and it lists the arXiv papers tied to that ORCID. It is the documented behaviour of the system, not a way around anything.

There are no papers to list. Nothing was posted to arXiv. This note is here so that the existence of the page is not mistaken for having been published on arXiv. What the page in fact displays has not been confirmed, because it cannot be opened from the working environment.

The philosophy papers are a different matter. PhilArchive is where readers in the field are, and that is where they are posted. It also has a stated professional standard, a reserved right of rejection, and more than six hundred editors. There is no need to move up a venue.

blocks.title: On calling this a ranking
blocks.html:
The venues themselves are not ranked. The only thing that can be ordered is whether a venue suits this work.

WorkVenue that suits itReason
The three Trinity-Infinity papersNone suits it. It goes to arXiv anywayThat what survives has no novelty is something the record says of itself, and the decision does not change that. It is posted in full knowledge that it does not fit. The outcome, rejection included, gets recorded
The three philosophy papersPhilArchiveThe readers in the field are there. And it is a place with a stated standard
The source noteZenodo and Knowledge CommonsIt is enough that the transcription and the citation are read
errata-checkA journal that peer reviews softwareWhat such review examines is whether it runs and whether it is documented, which is a fit. Not yet submitted

Looking for the venue that fits is quicker than looking for the strictest one. arXiv is a place for putting out new results; what is here is a record that keeps its mistakes rather than deleting them. They are different kinds of thing. How the decision to post anyway came about is in ARXIV.md.

blocks.title: What this page does not say
blocks.html:
• It does not compare the quality of the sites. What is compared is the acceptance rules
  • None of these venues is peer review. None of them judges whether the content holds
  • The descriptions of the rules are unconfirmed. They were taken from search results, not from the originals
  • No venue is being recommended. What is written is whether it fits
  • The date it is current as of is at the top of the page. Changes to the rules after that are not reflected

How to overturn this. Point to one place where a rule described above differs from the actual rule, and that line falls. One is enough.
